speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FAR EAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). In view of the protest of India at her exclusion from further Far East war criminal proceedings, as reported in the New York Times yesterday, would the minister state the Canadian government's position on this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: FAR EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should answer this question as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. The position of the Canadian government is that the power to grant clemency to and to parole persons sentenced by the international military tribunal for the Far East is determined by the terms of the Japanese peace treaty. Articles 11 and 25 of that treaty, when read together, confine the exercise of this power to the governments that have both signed and ratified the treaty of peace with Japan, that is, Australia, Canada, France, The Netherlands, New Zealand, Pakistan, the United Kingdom and the United States. If India had also signed and ratified the treaty of peace with Japan, India would have been eligible to participate in the exercise of clemency with respect to persons sentenced by the international military tribunal for the Far East.
This position was made known to the representative of the government of India in December last. Recently the Indian government informed the Canadian authorities that it found it necessary to reaffirm its objection to being excluded from participation. The position taken by the Canadian government remains unaltered, and I understand that a similar attitude has been taken by the other countries concerned.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARREST OF ALFRED VALDMANIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, of which I have given him notice. In view of the criticism in connection with the arrest of Alfred Valdmanis, and in fairness to the R.C.M.P. involved, would the minister care to make some statement in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARREST OF ALFRED VALDMANIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of his question.
T.C.A. flight 465 from Newfoundland, carrying Corporal Clark of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, with a warrant to apprehend Dr. Alfred Valdmanis, was delayed by weather conditions and arrived at Fredericton airport at 10.15 p.m. of April 22. By the time Corporal Clark had been driven in an R.C.M.P. highway patrol car to Peters-ville and thence to St. Andrews, it was approximately two a.m. of April 23.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Corporal Clark was accompanied by another member of the force and on arrival at St. Andrews they were joined by Constable Winter of the St. Andrews town detachment. All of them were in plain clothes. Constable Winter introduced them to the local police magistrate who backed the Newfoundland warrant. Proceeding at once to the home of Dr. Valdmanis' brother at Chamcook, they effected the arrest of Dr. Valdmanis and left the house at 3.20 a.m.
Corporal Clark's instructions had been to return immediately to Newfoundland after effecting the arrest, but owing to weather conditions the party could not leave according to schedule and did not leave until the afternoon of April 24, arriving at St. John's, Newfoundland, on the same date.
In view of the fact that this was an important case and that Chamcook, New Brunswick, is close to the United States boundary, it was considered the course of prudence to effect the arrest of Dr. Valdmanis as soon as possible after the backing of the Newfoundland warrant by the New Brunswick police magistrate.
While I am aware, as minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, that the arrest in this case has caused some criticism, I am of the opinion, in view of the importance of the prosecution and the large amount of money involved in the charges, that the arrest was handled with efficiency and discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the ratification by Canada of the agreement on commerce between Canada and Japan, signed at Ottawa on March 31, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.
He said:	An agreement on commerce
between the Canadian and the Japanese governments was signed in Ottawa on March 31. An announcement was made in the house at the same time and the text was released for publication. The agreement will enter into force when it has been ratified by both governments. Because of the exceptional importance of this agreement, and because of the widespread interest in it, a resolution has been tabled to obtain the approval of the house in advance of ratification.
It has appeared for some time to be in our national interest to work out a mutually advantageous trade agreement with Japan.

Trade Agreement with Japan

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext: Order. May I be permitted to interrupt the minister tor one second in order to ask hon. members tor their co-operation with respect to observing silence. It is very difficult to hear the minister, although normally he speaks loud enough, but if hon. members' conversation competes with his voice the loudspeaker system will be of no assistance at all, and I know many hon. members are interested in the question now before the house. I would ask hon. members if they wish to converse to do so in a very low voice or, which is better, use the lobbies which I think have been provided for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Japan has already become our third largest customer. It seems probable that Japan will continue in the future to increase in importance as a market for our exports.
Japan is assuming the status of a major participant in world trade. A great deal of reconstruction and reorganization has taken place in the Japanese economy since the end of the war. Certain aspects of these developments bear great promise for the future of our own trade.
This new agreement provides, among other things, for the exchange of most-favourednation treatment. This is the normal and established treatment which we extend to other friendly countries with which we trade. Quite clearly, we could not continue for much longer to withhold most-favoured-nation treatment from a country such as Japan, which is one of our largest customers.
In recent years we have been imposing the high rates of our general tariff upon imports from Japan. In consequence, we have imported very little from there, even though we have been selling large and increasing amounts of our exports to that country. It has become more and more difficult in these circumstances to justify the fact that we were not extending most-favoured-nation treatment to Japan. In the new trade agreement we are now proposing to correct this anomaly.
Hon. members know that the government is constantly helping to increase and diversify Canada's export trade overseas. On behalf of Canadian producers we attempt at every opportunity to improve the terms upon which our goods are admitted into the markets of other countries. We try to keep our trade agreements up-to-date. In this connection, this new trade agreement with Japan is an important step in strengthening our whole system of trade relations. It should provide a stable and beneficial basis for trade to take place between Canada and Japan.

In negotiating this new agreement, we set out to obtain and consolidate advantages in the Japanese market, and at the same time to safeguard in a reasonable way the position of our own Canadian manufacturers in our home market. The negotiations were carried on in Ottawa, over a considerable period of time, with representatives of the Japanese government. At each stage, the various aspects were given careful consideration by my cabinet colleagues and myself. The negotiations were recently concluded in a friendly way and both sides regarded the results as satisfactory. Good trade relations and effective trade agreements are based on the willingness of countries to recognize each other's difficulties. They are based also on the desire to make well-balanced arrangements which will operate to the advantage of all concerned.
Let me give a short outline of the essential features of the agreement, and I will then go into some explanatory details. Briefly, there are three important ways in which this agreement will facilitate the access of Canadian goods to the Japanese market. In the first place, our exports will be guaranteed most-favoured-nation treatment in Japan, Secondly, we will be assured that there will be no discrimination whatsoever against Canada and in favour of any other hard currency country with respect to quantitative restrictions, exchange controls, or any other matters. Thirdly, with respect to a list of nine important Canadian export products, Japan undertakes not to discriminate against Canada in favour of any other country regardless of its currency position. This list of products includes wheat, barley, wood-pulp, flaxseed, primary copper, lead in pigs, zinc spelter, synthetic resins and milk powders. These are all very important concessions to have received. I shall return to these points a little later, to explain them more fully.
On our side, we undertake to make certain concessions to Japan. The agreement provides that Canada will extend most-favourednation treatment to Japanese goods. This means that imports from Japan will be entered under our most-favoured-nation rates of duty, which are generally applicable to the non-commonwealth countries with which we trade. This will involve reductions in the duties on imports from Japan, which have hitherto been subject to the much higher rates set forth in our general tariff. It is, of course, to be predicted that imports from Japan will increase under these new arrangements.
4S49

In 1953, Japan purchased almost $119 million worth of Canadian goods. This total was exceeded only by our sales to the United States and to the United Kingdom. In the same year, Canada bought less than $14 million worth of goods from Japan. For every dollar Canadians spent on Japanese goods, in other words, the Japanese bought more than $8 worth in Canada. We could not reasonably expect to continue to enjoy such high sales to Japan if at the same time Japanese goods were to continue to be restricted from entry into Canada by the high rates of our general tariff. Japan legitimately expects to sell more in this country. For my part, I do not believe we need to be afraid of such increases. Under these new arrangements, Japan will be in a position to compete for a share of the Canadian market on an equal basis with other foreign suppliers, such as the United States and Germany. Importers may well find it advantageous to obtain some of their requirements from Japan in competition with their former sources of supply.
Canadian imports from Japan have increased in value as compared with pre-war years, but they are still relatively small. Last year, they included a range of items such as iron and steel, toys, oranges, pottery and chinaware, silk and other fabrics, tuna fish and a variety of manufactured products. Only in two items did our imports from Japan amount to as much as $1 million. Aside from these items, the value of individual import items from Japan was in each case considerably below a half million dollars.
When it is remembered that total imports into the Canadian market in 1953 amounted to $4-3 billion, it is clear that there is considerable scope for Japan, from its present level of $14 million, to obtain an increased share of our large import market. Out of every $100 worth of goods imported into Canada last year, about 30 cents' worth came from Japan. There is obviously room for a considerable increase in imports, which would contribute to a healthier balance of trade and at the same time be of such dimensions as to be readily absorbed.
In case injurious competition should materialize for particular Canadian industries out of such imports, careful safeguards have been provided in the agreement. We have been mindful of the fact that a sudden influx of low-priced imports might seriously affect some particular Canadian industry. In the agreement Canada therefore reserves the right to apply special duties on Japanese goods in legitimate cases of emergency where, as a result of increased imports, there is a serious threat of injury to domestic producers.
Trade Agreement with Japan
I hope, however, that Canadian trade with Japan will develop in such a way as not to create serious problems for Canadian industry. Japan, like ourselves, is vitally dependent on foreign trade. The Japanese government is no doubt fully aware of the fact that no lasting trade relations can be built up except on the basis of mutual good will and of adherence to fair trade practices. It is reasonable to expect that Japanese exporters will try to avoid creating problems which would undermine good relations. Japan has in recent years instituted a comprehensive system of control and inspection for its exports, in a positive effort to prevent dumping of goods, misrepresentation of trade marks and patents and other undesirable methods, and to abide by internationally accepted fair trade practices.
I shall go on now to explain in a little more detail some of the concessions we have received. It is important that we are now to be assured by Japan of most-favoured-nation treatment as regards tariffs and all related matters. Since the Japanese maintain at present a single-column tariff, this agreement does not have the immediate effect of lowering their rates of duty on Canadian goods. However, the Japanese tariff does provide for heavy surcharges on goods from countries which discriminate against Japan. It is also possible, of course, that Japan may in the future decide to revise its present tariffs. With respect to all such eventualities, this agreement assures Canadian exports of the lowest rates of duty and of the most favourable tariff treatment that may be accorded by Japan to any country.
We have recognized in this agreement that, in view of their continuing balance of payments problems, the Japanese may from time to time find it necessary to enforce certain import and exchange restrictions on a temporary basis. However, the agreement provides that Canadian exports to Japan shall receive treatment no less favourable than is accorded to our competitors in other dollar countries. There can be no discrimination of any kind against Canadian goods as compared with goods from other countries, such as the United States, whose currencies are convertible. This is an important guarantee which applies over the whole field of our exports to Japan.
In addition, the very significant concession is made by Japan of guaranteeing against all discriminatory restrictions whatsoever the list of nine important Canadian products, including wheat, which I have already enumerated and which make up a very high proportion of our trade with Japan. For these goods, Japan has undertaken to grant licences and
4650	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan exchange without regard to currency considerations. We are thus assured of our freedom to compete, on a normal commercial basis, with all other suppliers, wherever they may be and whatever currency they may use. There are certain agreed exceptions to this rule but they affect only a limited number of the nine commodities listed, and they apply only to specific quantities and for specific periods. These special exceptions have been provided to permit the Japanese government to fulfil undertakings it has entered into in trade agreements with certain other countries.
Last year Japan was our second largest market for wheat and it is also one of the leading markets for Canadian barley. The growth of Japanese imports of wheat and barley has been a remarkable development of recent years and constitutes in effect the creation of a new and continuing market for these basic Canadian exports. Our exports of wheat to Japan have increased from less than $1 million in 1949 to $52 million last year, representing almost 10 per cent of our total wheat exports. We sold about 800,000 tons of wheat to Japan in the last crop year and we expect to equal this performance in the current year. Similarly, while we sold no barley to Japan until three or four years ago, Japan last year purchased over $17 million of Canadian barley, representing almost 13 per cent of our total barley exports in 1953. Japan has become for the first time a major grain importing country.
This very significant increase in grain exports to Japan is not the result of temporary factors. On the contrary, the dietary changes that are taking place in Japan, the improved standard of living, and the development of an efficient milling industry in that country, all point to even higher levels of grain consumption in future years. Representatives of my department and of the Canadian wheat board, who visited Japan last January to discuss the grain trade, were very favourably impressed with the potentialities of the Japanese market. They were told that consumption of wheat flour in Japan in 1953 was 50 per cent higher than in 1952, and that the production of processed barley for human consumption in Japan in 1953 was 30 per cent greater than in the previous year. It is my belief that this increasing trend of Japanese requirements will continue. I am happy that Canada is in a position to supply a large proportion of these needs.
Japan is also one of Canada's major markets for woodpulp, for flaxseed, iron ore, copper and other important products. For example, Japan was our third largest market for dissolving pulp last year, taking 10 per cent of our total exports, and substantial


amounts of other grades of pulp were also shipped. Our exports of flaxseed to Japan in 1953 represented about 10 per cent of our total flaxseed exports. Non-ferrous metals were our leading exports to Japan before the war and Japan continues as a potentially important market for these products. Canada's expanding synthetic resin industry is also finding a valuable export market in Japan.
In fact, Japan, with her 85 million population and with her highly developed industries, is one of the world's largest markets for foodstuffs and raw materials, and for other products which we can supply. The maintenance of high levels of exports of these products is of fundamental importance to the whole Canadian economy. It is of direct benefit to our agriculture, our forest and our mining industries. By contributing to a buoyant economy and a prosperous domestic market in Canada, it is of vital importance to our own manufacturing industries which sell their products in the Canadian market. We have no monopoly on the supply of such products, of course, and other countries are also anxious to expand their share of the Japanese market.
Ratification of our agreement should open a new era of fruitful trade relations between Canada and Japan. Our two economies are to a large degree complementary and have much to gain from close and constructive co-operation. We are happy to play our part in helping Japan to take her place as a partner in the world trading community.
It will be recalled that at the last session of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade in Geneva, Canada voted in favour of inviting Japan to participate in the work of the contracting parties. This did not, of course, mean full membership for Japan; nor did it mean that Canada and Japan undertook the rights and obligations of the agreement with respect to each other. We also indicated at that time, however, that we were negotiating a trade agreement with Japan and that, once a satisfactory agreement had been concluded, and subject to the terms of that agreement, the Canadian government would be prepared to consider bringing the GATT into effect as between Canada and Japan.
Subject to the terms of this new agreement, we intend to apply the GATT to our trade relations with Japan, thus joining with the other GATT countries which have decided to bring their trade relations with Japan within that framework. It should be noted that our agreement with Japan already

contains many of the essential features provided for in the GATT, with respect to mostfavoured-nation treatment in tariffs and other matters. This new agreement is in fact somewhat stronger and more specific than the present provisions of the GATT with respect to the non-discriminatory application of exchange and import controls. Similarly, the Canadian government's right to adopt safeguarding measures against unfair or injurious competition is established in a more precise and explicit manner in the agreement with Japan than it is under the corresponding provisions of the GATT. At the same time, we regard the agreement with Japan as being consistent in all respects with the principles of the GATT.
Hon. members will recall that when I announced in the house the signing of the agreement on March 31, I pointed out that its importance goes beyond commercial considerations. This agreement should contribute to stable and friendly relations between the two countries and to the peace, security and progress of the Pacific area. 1 am confident that this agreement will prove to be in the long-run interests of both Canada and Japan. I would remind the house that other important trading countries are taking steps to consolidate their trade relations with Japan. The United Kingdom government has recently renewed and to some extent liberalized its payments agreement with Japan. The United States, which already has a most-favourednation agreement, has indicated that it contemplates tariff negotiations with Japan and it is seeking special authority for such negotiations.
We have tried to obtain a carefully formulated and well balanced agreement which should go a long way in itself to reassure those of our producers who are afraid of being seriously hurt. When we think of the present importance and the potential growth of the Japanese market for many of our export products, there can be no doubt of where our interest lies. This agreement will help over the years to provide employment and income in agriculture, in our forest and mining industries and in other industries across the country. For these reasons I hope the resolution will receive cordial and widespread support.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that no member of the house entertains any doubt about the importance of the measure now before us. Trade is a factor of high importance in the outlook of this country both with respect to peace and our economic future and, indeed, the whole development of this country with
Trade Agreement with Japan which Providence has blessed us. Our trade and economic relations with Japan must, in the light of existing conditions in the world and in the light of our trade and economic relations with that country in the past, claim a place of high importance in the consideration of hon. members of this house.
In the resolution submitted to the house, Mr. Speaker, the house is invited to express its approval of the ratification of the trade agreement signed by Canada and Japan on March 31, 1954. May I point out, sir, that the procedure does have the effect of restricting consideration of this measure. This is a debate on a resolution. Only one stage of discussion is afforded. I should think with any measure of such great importance it would have been desirable, were it possible, for the measure to receive careful consideration in a committee of the house where it would be possible for hon. members to ask those many questions which naturally arise in their minds in relation to a trade treaty of such high importance. It would also permit those who have views to express to do so.
I recall, sir, that in the session of 1948, when the general agreement on tariffs and trade which had been signed at Geneva in the fall of 1947 was brought to the house for ratification, the government did follow a suggestion that I think came from Mr. Bracken, the then leader of the opposition, that the treaty, after an initial debate, should be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce for further consideration. In that committee the matter was given more detailed consideration and was the subject of a more informal discussion than is ever possible in a debate in this house. Indeed, sir, the procedure that we are following today is such that it is not possible to ask the government any of the questions which I am sure crowd into the minds of hon. members in relation to so important a matter.
This subject, sir, can only be fairly considered against a background which must embrace our consideration of our economic and political relations with Japan in the past. The history of our pre-war trade relations with Japan is, frankly, not altogether happy. The mention of trade with Japan to those who recall the conditions attendant upon our trade with Japan in pre-war years is to invite the recollection of the days when Japanese goods, particularly textiles and toys, flooded the Canadian market and undersold Canadian products by reason of the very low standard of living of the Japanese people and the Japanese workman in particular, in comparison with our own.

Trade Agreement with Japan
Then, of course, came the war. To think of the war, of course, is to invite the recollection of deep wounds. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I think we would not be true to the trust imposed in us as legislators of Canada, nor would we be true to the responsibility that rests upon Canada as a great democratic nation in the world today, if we did not believe that those deep wounds inflicted from 1941 to 1945 are capable of being healed, and that it may be possible to restore to our relations with Japan that healthy mutual regard that did once exist.
We recall, sir, that Canada and Japan entered into a treaty of peace two years ago. We recall that it was generous in its terms. We recall that it followed a treaty of peace between the United States and Japan which was signal in the generosity of the terms extended by the victor to the defeated1 nation. This house on June 16, 1952, gave unanimous approval to this treaty of peace and the ensuing legislative measures. Why did we do this, Mr. Speaker? Why did we seek to be generous in the terms of the treaty of peace we approved with Japan at that time? I am certain that one factor that was high in the consideration of hon. members of this house was our hope that Japan would come to hold a position of respect and mutual regard amongst the democratic nations of the world. We wanted to leave no stone in the path of Japan taking that kind of position amongst the civilized nations of the world. The behaviour of the Japanese government and nation since the war has been such as to encourage the hopes we expressed at that time.
The Japanese government has sought to follow a path of co-operation with the western nations. The Japanese government did not, as her own economic interest might have dictated, recognize the communist, so-called people's government of China. It chose rather on June 18, 1952, to recognize the existing nationalist government of China. She applied to become a member of the United Nations, and would have become a member had not the Russian delegate on September 18, 1952, exercised the 52nd Russian veto to defeat Japan's application for membership in the United Nations. Last December Japan became a party to the statutes of the international court of justice. Only Russia abstained in the voting in the security council and the assembly.
The hope of the western world in a substantial degree in that quarter of the globe can fairly be said to be put upon the basis that Japan is, and shall continue to be, the major outpost against communism. It is proper, sir, that we should have regard to the


political and economic conditions existing in Japan today. I affirm that these are matters of concern to us. We cannot take a narrow approach to questions of this kind. If conditions in Japan, either in the political or economic field, were to suffer drastic deterioration, who can say how long it would be before communism would rear its ugly head and challenge the government? In so far as political conditions are concerned, it may be unwise to say more than that at the moment the government in Japan is not in a too strong position. But we may properly examine, and in greater detail it seems to me, the economic conditions subsisting today in Japan. The economic conditions today are not too sound.
Japan is a nation confined within narrow geographical boundaries. She is poor in the possession of natural resources. Her economy is such that she must depend upon export trade for her economic health. Only 16 per cent of the soil of Japan is arable. Next to The Netherlands and Belgium, Japan has the densest population in all the world in relation to her arable land. The population in Japan is 3,600 per square mile, and the total population today is about 86 million. It is increasing at the net rate of 1,200,000 per year. It is estimated that by 1960 the population of Japan will have increased to 95 million people. In very truth, sir, Japan is bulging at the seams. As a result of the war she no longer has those colonies with which she had built up a very substantial trade before the war. Japanese immigrants are not being received in numbers in other parts of the world. The United States is now receiving about 150 per annum, and the number that Canada receives is, of course, slightly smaller.
Before the war 42 per cent of Japan's exports went to China, Formosa and Korea. She has been stripped of her colonies and her loss in that regard is serious when we look at the trade she enjoyed with Formosa and Korea as well as Manchuria. As a result of the war she lost her colonies, which constituted 46 per cent of her pre-war territory.
There are other disturbing features in the economy of Japan today. As a result of the stress of war and post-war conditions, inflation has been rampant in Japan. Taking 1937 as a base of 100, her wholesale prices by the middle of 1952 had jumped, according to official Japanese statistics, to 27,300. The cost of living in Japan has soared to very great heights and taxes are very high. Interest rates are abnormally high. Indeed, the Japanese economy has been maintained in effect by United States assistance-United States assistance in the form of direct aid and

in the procurement policies followed in relation to the occupation of Japan by American troops, and in the hostilities in Korea.
By late 1953 Japanese exports were only 31 per cent of what they were in pre-war days. Her imports then were just 54 per cent of what they were in pre-war days. The ratio of her total trade volume to national income is 22 per cent today as against a pre-war percentage of 37 per cent. The average annual income per capita in Japan is $150. It is the highest in Asia but it is very low compared with the Canadian income of roughly $1,000 per capita.
United States aid to Japan has been indeed substantial. From the end of the war up to September 30, 1953, net grants for economic aid from the United States to Japan were $2,439 million. Those figures are for direct aid alone. Even with the substantial procurement policy followed by the United States in Japan that country in 1952 suffered a visible trade deficit of $570 million. Allowance, of course, must be made for certain invisible figures in the trade accounts, but Japan's trade position today is unbalanced. She has had to resort to import restrictions and other protective devices.
Japan's exchange position must be as well a matter of concern. She has suffered from a lack of foreign exchange-sterling in particular. This is in part the result of import restrictions which existed until recently in the colonies of the British Empire. On September 20,	1953, Japan's holdings of
foreign exchange had been reduced to the equivalent of $1,008 million United States dollars, of which $872 million were in the form of United States dollars.
Japan has been seeking to expand her exports. In 1953 she partially lifted the ban on exports to Red China and placed a number of carefully selected items on a so-called free list. The trade volume under those special arrangements is expected to reach a volume of only $15 million on a strict barter basis.
These, it seems to me, are all important considerations in approaching a trade treaty between our country and Japan. Before the war Japan had a very great market in Asia. Her pre-war market in Asia accounted for 64 per cent of her total exports. That figure dropped in 1951 to 51 per cent. This has had a very restrictive effect upon the Japanese economy. We must take account of that factor because it is the political factors in which we have direct and lively concern which are responsible in substantial measure for the curtailment of the markets formerly enjoyed by Japan in Asia.
Then, sir, what of our own trade relations with Japan? I do not wish to weary the
Trade Agreement with Japan house with statistics, but it seems to me that an intensive study of the trade figures pertaining to our trade with Japan in recent years is extremely illuminating. On the import side the average figure for Canadian imports from Japan from 1935 to 1939 was $4,649,000. In 1939, the last pre-war year, the figure had risen to only $4,864,000. By 1948, when conditions were becoming more settled in the East, our imports from Japan were just $3,144,000. They increased in 1949 to $5,551,000. In 1950 they were $12,086,627; in 1951 $12,577,000; in 1952 $13,162,000; and in 1953, $13,629,000.
There has been, it will be seen, a substantial increase in these post-war years over any figures that had existed up to that time. The figures have been relatively stable during the past four years.
What now of our exports to Japan? The pre-war average, from 1935 to 1939, of our exports to Japan was $21,880,000. 1 give only the round figures. In 1939, the last pre-war year, we exported to Japan $28,168,000 worth of goods. In 1948 when, as I mentioned, conditions became more settled, we exported to Japan $8 million worth of goods. In 1949 that figure dropped to $5,860,000. In 1950 we advanced the figure to $20,533,000. In 1951 there was a huge increase to $73 million, and the increase has continued since. In 1952 the figure was $102 million and in 1953 an all-time high was recorded of $118,500,000.
Sir, the nature of our commodity trade with Japan, as the minister has indicated, is a matter of high importance in our consideration of this subject today. Wheat has been our leading commodity export to Japan. Last year we exported some $52 million worth of wheat to Japan. Our barley exports have been a feature of our trade with Japan during the last several years. In 1952 we exported $39 million worth of barley. In 1953 that dropped to $17,500,000. Our export of wood pulp sulphite and wood pulp sulphate, which go into the making of Japanese rayon, advanced from $6 million in 1952 to something over $8 million in 1953. Our exports of copper, ore, and scrap advanced in 1953 to $4,300,000. Our scrap iron or steel advanced in 1953 to $3,862,000, and flaxseed from a mere $27,000 in 1952 to $1,380,000 in round figures in 1953.
It will be seen, sir, that our trade with Japan, both import and export, has now reached all-time records. The second striking feature of these figures is the extraordinary imbalance of our trade with Japan. Now, even making allowance for the invisible figures that should enter into our consideration of any of the figures on visible exports and imports, the fact is that for some time we

Trade Agreement with Japan have been selling to Japan eight times as much as we have been buying from her.
Among the best customers of Canada Japan in 1950 stood ninth, in 1952 fourth, and in 1953 third. This has been at a time when on the continent of Asia there has been an increasing tendency towards independence or self-sufficiency in trade matters on the part of countries there, and Japan, which is more dependent upon export trade than any other nation in Asia, has naturally felt the adverse effects of that policy on the continent of Asia.
We must now look, sir, at conditions in our own country which may be affected by the terms of this treaty. Sir, textiles and steel products, electrical goods and pottery are likely to play a leading part in the export hopes and plans of the Japanese people under the terms of this treaty.
It is an unhappy, an inescapable fact, I suppose, that in the last nearly decade and a half this is perhaps the most unfavourable time for the Canadian textile industry and the other industries I have just mentioned to face the rigour of Japanese competition in the Canadian market. It is an inescapable fact that not one more textile import today is needed to hurt the Canadian industry. Canadian industry has suffered a good deal of economic deterioration in recent months. Let us then examine the treaty in the light of this background.
I do not wish to review the ground which the minister has covered in his speech this afternoon. The purpose of the treaty, as has been stated, is to offer unconditional mostfavoured-nation treatment in all matters on a mutual basis between the two countries. There are exceptions. One exception of course is made in article I, paragraph 5, which stipulates that the agreement is not to affect the advantages accorded by Canada to members of the British commonwealth of nations. Then we have in article III, paragraph 3, some provisions that may come to play a very important part in the effect of this Japanese trade treaty; that is, the provision in relation to balance of payments.
In considering the weaknesses of many of the nations of the world today in relation to their exchange position we should have due consideration for the effect of this article. It provides, sir, that:
Both contracting parties recognize that the existence of balance of payments difficulties in many countries, and the widespread inconvertibility of currencies, do not permit the immediate and full achievement of non-discriminatory application of trade and exchange restrictions affecting imports.

And for that reason provision is made in this article that either contracting party may:
... in the application of trade or exchange restrictions affecting imports for the purpose of safeguarding its external financial position and balance of payments, temporarily deviate from the provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article-
-on two conditions which are in the form of a proviso:
Provided that:
(a)	its restrictions shall be applied in such a way as to avoid unnecessary damage to the commercial or economic interests of the other contracting party;
(b)	its restrictions shall not be applied in such a way as to result directly or indirectly in discrimination as between countries which are treated as part of the United States dollar area under its exchange control regulations, or as between countries whose currencies are or become convertible in the hands of persons who are treated as nonresidents under the exchange control regulations of the countries concerned.
The next article of direct concern to us in this debate, sir, is article V, in relation to the maintenance of fair trade practices. It provides:
Each contracting party undertakes to conform in its trade and commerce to internationally accepted fair practices, particularly in matters relating to trade marks, marks of origin and rights under patents, and to co-operate with the other contracting party with a view to preventing any practices which might prejudicially affect the commerce between the two countries.
Article VII defines the duration of the agreement. It is to continue in effect for a period of one year from its entry into force, and thereafter until three months from the date on which either of the parties shall have given notice to the other of the intention to terminate the agreement.
The correspondence which has been exchanged between the contracting parties on March 31, 1954, has also been made a part of the treaty by protocol. One of the letters written by the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) contains a provision which I suppose, in the view of many of us in this house, will be regarded as of crucial importance, for under its provisions Canada "reserves the right to establish values for ordinary and special purposes in the following terms." I do not propose to read these terms, sir, with the exception of one paragraph, and I do read it in extenso because of its importance:
If, as a result of unforeseen developments and of the effect of the obligations incurred by Canada under the aforesaid agreement, any product is being imported into its territory in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic producers in its territory of like or directly competitive products, Canada will be free, In respect of

such product, and to the extent and for such a time as may be necessary to prevent or remedy such injury, to establish values for ordinary and special duty purposes.
Canada's right to proceed in that manner is recognized by the next following letter from the ambassador of Japan. Then in the following letter the government of Japan undertakes to accord unconditional non-discriminatory treatment with respect to the importation into Japan of nine designated commodities, namely, wheat, barley, wood-pulp, flaxseed, primary copper, lead in pigs, zinc spelter, synthetic resins and milk powder.
Sir, the safeguards to which Canadian industries will look are undoubtedly those in relation, first of all, to the duration of the agreement; second, those in relation to the maintenance of fair trade practices; third, the provision that I have read in regard to the imposition of special duties in certain cases. Most-favoured-nation status is to all intents and purposes the same status as any nation derives under GATT. There is one further feature as well, that the legislation passed in this house in December last in amending the Customs Act will have application to imports from Japan as well as the provision which I have read in relation to the establishment of special duties.
I make just this comment on the importance and value of those safeguards, sir. First of all, in regard to duration, if it should happen that for any reason the treaty proves to be a disappointment and this house desires that steps be taken either to terminate the agreement or to seek changes in it, it will not be a very easy matter to terminate it. Hon. members may say, "Well, all you need to do is to give notice." But the fact of the matter is that in the relations of one country with another the sudden termination of trade treaties oftentimes provokes unhappy differences, and it is not the sort of thing any country in times like these desires to do to a country with which it is seeking to foster friendly and close relations.
As to the value of the provision in relation to the establishment of special values for commodity purposes, I would draw your attention, sir, to what may be considered a somewhat narrowing provision. It is to be observed that this clause can be invoked only as the result of unforeseen developments and the effect of obligations incurred by Canada under the agreement on products being imported into Canada in such increased amounts and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to Canadian domestic producers.
Let me stress that this clause can be invoked only where the unhappy results contemplated by this provision arise as the result
Trade Agreement with Japan of "unforeseen developments". Now, I do not know that any hon. members of this house can say that a very substantial increase in Japanese imports into Canada, and not least in those commodities where there is substantial unemployment today in Canada, will be unforeseen. I think it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that there is going to be a substantial increase in Canadian importation of Japanese products, and therefore I put it before the house that under this provision, which has been stressed by the minister both in the statement he made today and the statement he made in this house on March 31, and has been stressed in the thinking of many people and the writings of some in relation to this Japanese treaty, the right can be invoked by Canada only where the unhappy conditions contemplated of a threat of injury to the Canadian domestic producer is unforeseen today.
Now, sir, I pass on to examine this treaty in terms of the ledger balance. It does undoubtedly offer benefits and against those benefits we must weigh whatever cost there may be to Canada.
In the face of the condition of imbalance in trade with Japan, to which I have made reference, it is quite clear that even if we were to achieve by this treaty no more than an assurance of a continuation of the kind of market we have been enjoying in Japan, it would have important value for Canada. Canada is to achieve most-favoured-nation status in the Japanese market. But the minister has not said, as I followed his statement today, that Canada is likely to increase her exports to Japan in any substantial measure. He did lay stress today on the maintenance, through the instrumentality of this treaty, of the position that Canada enjoys in the Japanese market today. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while we would like to see this treaty made the means of increasing our sales to Japan of Canadian goods, I think it well to remind ourselves that that hope has not been expressly held out today by the minister. Of course, it will remain with Canadian businessmen and the Canadian wheat board to take advantage of the position that is ensured to Canada under this treaty for its duration.
We would like to see Japan substantially increase her purchases of Canadian wheat. Her record purchases of wheat amounting to $52 million last year, and $17 million worth of Canadian barley, may give us hope that we will be able to enlarge the sale of these important commodities to Japan. With the surplus of wheat which exists in Canada today we hope that the dietary trend in Japan, which has been moving people more and more from the position of rice eaters to the position of wheat consumers, will continue. We wish naturally to be in the

Trade Agreement with Japan forefront of the sale of wheat in the Japanese market. I leave this matter of the benefits to Canada, Mr. Speaker, simply with this note of warning, that the minister has not indicated or has not held out any glowing hope of an increase in Canadian sales to Japan.
On the import side there are many commodities undoubtedly which will be available to the Canadian consumer at lower prices, but I ask the house to consider this also in relation to the other side of the ledger balance of this treaty. The effect of extending most-favoured-nation treatment to Japan under this treaty will be to reduce the present tariff rates on the products concerned. Gloves will be reduced from 45 per cent under the general tariff to 25 per cent under most-favoured-nation treatment; toys, 40 per cent today, will be 25 per cent under the treaty; pure silk clothing, 45 per cent today plus seven cents per ounce, will be 30 per cent under the treaty; pottery and china-ware, 35 per cent today under the general tariff, will be 20 or 25 per cent under the treaty, depending on the particular commodity.
Now, sir, what of the other side of the ledger balance? Perhaps we can consider this best in relation to the Japanese hopes of the benefits which will accrue to them under the treaty. There have been statements from high sources in Japan indicating that the Japanese hope to double their exports to Canada. If they double their exports to Canada it will mean increasing their exports to us to something like $25 million a year. The opinion that one may form in relation to this subject, Mr. Speaker, is that the Japanese hopes must be set much higher than that. The hopes of Japan with respect to increased exports into the Canadian market are centred largely in the field of textiles, steel products, and, of course, the extension of those sales to Canada with which she has been successful in the past, toys, cameras, tuna fish, oranges, pottery and ceramic products, and she hopes to extend her sales of shirts and gloves to Canada.
What has been the reaction in Canada to this treaty? It is only natural, sir, that the Canadian textile industry should demonstrate very serious concern about the treaty. Statements came from the Canadian textile industry when the treaty was announced objecting to it and contending it was unjust. The statement issued by the Primary Textiles Institute reads as follows:
It is unjust that the textile industry is apparently to bear the main brunt of increased Canadian imports from Japan, now that a trade treaty is being signed. This comes at a time when imported textiles already hold a commanding share of the Canadian market.


Japan has already become the world's largest textile exporter. Low wages, skilled workers and a completely rebuilt modern industry has restored them to that position within a few post-war years. Japan has captured this position by selling great volumes at low prices and will not be content with any small sales in Canada now that tariffs on many of their textiles are to be sharply reduced.
This statement proceeds to draw attention to the fact that "Japanese textiles packaged in clear imitation of well known Canadian brands are a recent example" of what are described as unfair practices.
Another is a "dual price system" whereby Japan sells products abroad for less than the price at home, described by the Manchester Guardian as a "flagrantly unfair system".
That is the end of my quotation from the statement from the Primary Textiles Institute of March 31.
I was interested in what that statement had to say about the existence of a two-price system in Japan. On looking into the matter further I found this statement in a recent review of economic conditions in Japan published in the Oriental Economist of February, 1954. This is a Tokyo publication in the English language. In it I find this paragraph:
Yet, from around the autumn 1952, certain items began to be quoted at lower levels for export than in the domestic market; and since early 1953, the gap between domestic and export prices has tended to widen appreciably. This dual price problem is particularly bad with cotton piece goods, rayon, galvanized sheet, ammonium sulphate, non-ferrous metals, vessels, and certain other items.
Mr. Speaker, as I understand the provisions of the treaty in relation to fair trade practices it will be the duty of the government to see that this dual price system is not used by Japanese exporters for the purpose of selling goods in Canada at a lower price than that which exists in Japan. If that is not the effect of the provisions of the treaty, then I think the minister owes it to the house to make a clear statement on this subject of the two prices.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I interject that our dumping laws are explicit on that point. In other words, if sales are made in the export market at prices lower than those in the domestic market, the provisions of the dumping act would apply.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister will have to go beyond that statement. If he will recall the discussion we had in this house last December on the government's amendment to the Customs Act, he will find that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) denied that a sale in the market of origin at a lower price than that which existed in Canada would be conclusive evidence of dumping. I think the minister must go beyond that. It seems to me that the

government must either give much more resolute and realistic interpretation to the Customs Act or it must make some use of the safeguards in this treaty to which I have made reference this afternoon. If we have entered into this treaty with the knowledge that there exists in Japan today a dual price system in the case of those commodities that are going to be exported in increasing quantities to Canada, then it cannot be said to be an unforeseen development if, as a result of those increased exports to Canada, conditions of acute economic distress follow here.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I still think that statement of the minister does not go the full length of giving the assurance the house should have on this point. subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the minister's statement does not agree with my understanding of the practice followed by the Canadian government in its valuation, and as that practice was interpreted by the government ministers last December in participating in that debate.
I have drawn attention to this matter of the dual price system, Mr. Speaker. It is within the knowledge of the government and I think it will be the intention of this house to hold the government accountable for seeing to it that Canadian products are 83276-295
Trade Agreement with Japan not permitted to be prejudiced by the existence in Japan of a dual price system, or any attempted continuation of it.
I was speaking of the reaction in Canada that followed the announcement of this treaty. Canadian labour has expressed itself. Even before the treaty was announced, but when it was understood that negotiations were approaching a consummation, Mr. Bengough, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, expressed fears in regard to the treaty, particularly for labour in the textile industry. He urged more consideration before any action was taken to admit more freely into the Canadian market Japanese textile products manufactured under conditions that cannot be compared with our Canadian standard of living. These fears that have been expressed, to which I have made reference, and others as well, emphasize the importance of those reservations and safeguards in the treaty to which I have already alluded. I repeat that we in Canada do not need to import one more textile product in order to create unemployment. Unemployment of serious proportions exists here today. Toy manufacturers have expressed their concern as well. They have drawn attention to the fact that in a recent publication, under authentic sources, average wage rates in Japan last September were shown to be 16-8 cents per hour compared with average wage rates in Canada of $1.10 per hour.
In our approach to this problem we naturally must have regard for what is being done in other countries. What is the United States doing to make it possible for the Japanese to sell more of their products abroad? I have already made reference to the fact that the United States has been most generous in outright economic aid, in giving to the Japanese up to September 30, 1953, since the end of the war net grants totalling $2,439 million. In 1951 United States commodity exports to Japan amounted to $592 million and United States imports from Japan amounted to $204 million. In 1952 United States exports to Japan amounted to $620 million and United States imports from Japan amounted to $226 million. The figures for 1953 are not yet available, but the estimate for 1953, based upon actual figures for the first six months of the year, indicates that United States exports to Japan in 1953 will amount to $574 million and United States imports from Japan to $250 million. That indicates that the United States is increasing somewhat its imports from Japan, but the United States is still selling to Japan far more than twice as much as she is buying from Japan. The United States gave Japan
4658	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan most-favoured-nation treatment by the peace treaty signed between those two countries in September, 1951. The peace treaty included economic provisions that had the effect of a trade treaty. That treaty was superseded by a regular trade treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation signed in April, 1953, which went into effect on November 4, 1953. That treaty included the same trade provisions as the peace treaty.
Now, sir, there are voices being raised in the United States warning that country that she must increase her imports from Japan if she would see the economy of Japan maintained in sufficient strength, in the face of a rapidly increasing population, to stand the economic rigours in the world of 1954. A press dispatch from Washington of February 23 last reports that Walter S. Robertson, assistant secretary of state for Far Eastern affairs, had testified to the house appropriations committee that he believed an outlet must be found for Japanese trade "or we will inevitably throw Japan into the communist orbit". Then the quotation proceeds:
"X think we should be doing everything within our power to develop trade for the Japanese throughout southeast Asia", he said. "We must have the co-operation of the British to do this. I think we have to be willing to open our markets and accept Japanese goods here in America to a greater extent than we are doing. It poses a very difficult problem for us. It poses political problems on which there are great differences of opinion".
Undoubtedly, sir, there will be great differences of opinion in the United States over increased imports from Japan, and it remains to be seen whether the United States will follow the high note struck by Mr. Walter Robertson in his testimony before the house appropriations committee on that occasion. Canada does not want to be found wanting in taking her fair and rightful share of the burden and responsibilities of assisting, in the world in which we live today, in promoting a degree of health in the Japanese economy when we consider the strategic position that that country holds in east Asia. But, sir, I do not think that we propose to prejudice the interests of Canadian workmen unless the United States is prepared to take her full share of the burden and responsibility.
What of the United Kingdom? The United Kingdom, after the difficult trade and balance of exchange position that developed in 1951 and 1952, took steps to impose restrictions against the importation of Japanese exports into British colonial markets, particularly those in southeast Asia. That was done in view of the difficulties facing the whole sterling group. On January 29, 1954 it was felt by the government of the United Kingdom that conditions had sufficiently improved


to warrant their signing a new agreement with Japan. It was discussed in the British House of Commons on February 1, 1954. The agreement did remove the restrictions that had been imposed on Japanese imports into the British colonial markets, and it meant of course that the advantage that had been enjoyed under those restrictions by the textile and pottery manufacturers in particular of the United Kingdom was gone.
There was a substantial outcry in the United Kingdom over this treaty, particularly from the textile and pottery industries, and it was attacked by the Labour opposition in the House of Commons. Nevertheless the position taken by the British government was that regard had to be had for the position of Japan and that the British government was not justified in continuing to impose import restrictions in the British colonial areas against imports from Japan. While I do not propose to dwell on the subject, I do draw attention to the fact that the British government, taking note of the fact that the sterling area had sold to Japan in the previous year twice as much as the sterling area had purchased from Japan, decided that it must face up to the fact that a way had to be found to permit the Japanese to sell more goods abroad in the sterling area.
Now, sir, I come to my conclusion, and I apologize to the house for having been so long in coming to it. I can only say in extenuation that this is a matter of high importance on which I think none of us can come to a conclusion without very careful regard for all of the factors I have sought to lay before the house today.
How should the house react to the resolution now submitted to us? Sir, I cannot dismiss from my mind measures such as the Colombo plan and the spirit in which we entered into them. Under the Colombo plan we took note of the economic conditions in the three self-governing nations of the British commonwealth in Asia. We indicated that we Canadians were prepared to take a share of the responsibility of assisting those sister nations to strengthen their economies. It is quite true that the Japanese trade treaty is not quite the same kind of plan as the Colombo plan. We are not being asked to make gifts to Japan. Nevertheless there are some facets of the spirit of the Colombo plan that it seems to me are directly relevant to our consideration of the Japanese trade treaty.
We took account then of the necessity of strengthening the economies of free nations in Asia, knowing that on the northern border of India today stands communist China, having swallowed up Tibet. We took account

also of the pressures upon the economies of those countries. We took account of the fact that the communist party is active today in countries like India and Ceylon. We thought that we had some share of responsibility for trying to assist democracy in those countries to survive these attacks of a sinister, cruel and materialistic creed. We believed that we could make a contribution to the peace of the world through better trade relations.
Are we justified today, sir, in shutting out Japan from our consideration in matters of that kind? It seems to me that, while we do not put Japan in the same position as we do our sister nations of the commonwealth in Asia, the spirit that dictated the action that we have taken in making annual contributions through the Colombo plan cannot be dismissed from our minds in relation to the resolution before us today.
All of us here believe that we can make a contribution to better understanding, to more friendly relations between the peaceful nations of the world if there is trade between them on a proper basis. I believe, therefore, that in deference to our responsibility to make Japan feel there is a place for her amongst the democratic nations of the world, we must take account of the necessity of maintaining a degree of health in the economy of Japan which depends so substantially upon export trade for her economic survival.
The second factor that I mention in this conclusion, sir, is this. We have entered into an era of competition such as we have not known for a decade and a half. The atmosphere of world trade is going to be far more competitive in these days immediately ahead of us than it has been since the outbreak of war in 1939. Britain is finding it today. Germany, due to the tremendous exertions of the German people in this postwar period, is a factor in the export markets of the world today, far greater than we have experienced since 1939. Now Japan, under this treaty, will possess a position in the Canadian market that will enable her to come into the most direct form of competition with Canadian products. It will be a calamity for all Canada if rigidity in the Canadian economy, high costs of production including the high cost of government, prevent the Canadian producers from meeting that competition on fair terms.
In this respect I should like to quote from a statement that appeared recently in a newspaper that is normally regarded as favourable to this government. It is the Ottawa Citizen of April 2, 1954, commenting directly on this treaty. It says:
Rather than respond by giving Canadian manufacturers additional tariff protection, the Canadian 83276-295J
Trade Agreement with Japan
government might well consider revising downward its own sales taxes. This would put Canadian business in a better position to compete with American goods, and incidentally with those from Japan and other outside sources. It is true that the lost revenues must be made up. Apart from resort to higher taxes in other fields, the government might find itself taking in more money from taxes at the reduced level, because of the stimulating effect on domestic business.
If Canadian producers-and I am thinking principally of Canadian workmen-find themselves confronted by competition from Japan which they find to be unfair, then I say that the government will have to bear its full share of responsibility for what it contributes through high cost of government and high taxes towards high Canadian costs of production.
There is one matter that I think should also be mentioned, Mr. Speaker. It is not a matter of the same far-reaching importance and extent as the matters I have just mentioned, but I do recall that the Canadian Manufacturers Association, in a submission to the government on November 12, 1953, on this subject, among other recommendations, said this:
That a marking provision be incorporated into the agreement-
That was the forthcoming trade agreement between Canada and Japan.
. . . requiring that all fully-finished manufactured Japanese goods be marked, stamped, branded or labelled in legible English or French words, in a conspicuous place, so as to indicate the country of. origin. In advancing this proposal we desire to point out that all goods which are imported into the United States from Japan are required to be clearly marked with an indication of the country of origin.
It is no disparagement of the Japanese to say that they are great imitators. For that reason, as well as for other reasons that are too obvious to require mention now, I do urge that effect should be given to that recommendation that was submitted to the government last November.
The safeguards under this treaty which have been stressed by the minister, both today and on March 31, are something that we rely upon in giving our support today to the treaty. These safeguards can remain simply a dead letter, a jumble of words in this treaty, unless there is and will be on the part of our government a resolute determination to make these safeguards effective for the purpose for which they have been written into this treaty and for which we are relying upon them today. If they are permitted to remain a dead letter, if the kind of occasion contemplated by these safeguards arises, then we will be calling this government to account. In the meantime, we say to the government we are taking due note
4660	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan of these reservations and safeguards. You have stressed them in asking the house to give adherence to this treaty. We are relying upon your assurance. We look to you to make that assurance good one hundred per cent.
Then, sir-and this is perhaps something that confronts any opposition in relation to a government measure of this kind in recognizing its far-reaching	importance-the
government has, by a series of secret negotiations, arrived at an agreement with the Japanese government. The country was told singularly little, indeed nothing of any importance, about the course of these negotiations. We do not even know who were the negotiators on behalf of Canada. The government, with the knowledge that is available to it in the departments of government principally concerned, has chosen to enter into this treaty and to ask the house to approve it. A very heavy measure of responsibility consequently rests upon the government.
We in this house can deal with this only In general terms, in principle, and it is on the basis of principle that I have approached the treaty today. I remind the house again, and I hope if questions later arise the country will bear this in mind, that all that is afforded :in this House of Commons in relation to this treaty is an opportunity at one stage today to discuss the treaty in general terms. There is no opportunity afforded to us to ask questions, to dig into this question and that question that naturally arise in relation to the treaty. We have no opportunity to question the minister. We have no opportunity to question the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of External Affairs. The government takes the responsibility for negotiating this treaty. It takes the responsibility for asking the house to approve the treaty. We are prepared to do so in principle with the reliance that I have indicated that we place upon the solemn assurances given to us-and it is on that basis and that basis alone that we proceed today.
Finally, sir, may I express the hope that I am sure is entertained by every hon. member in this house, that in approving this treaty today we are not unmindful of the problems involved, we are not unmindful of the problem it presents particularly to producers of Canadian textiles, steel products, electrical products, and others of the various categories that I have mentioned, we are not unmindful of the responsibility that will rest upon us as an opposition to see to it, so far as we can, that the government is reminded whenever occasion arises of the


responsibility that it assumes under this agreement to make those safeguards effective.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, it is I know in the mind of every member of this house that we today, in an angry, tumultuous world, a world in which there is still so much of strife, of discord and bloodshed, may somehow through this means make a contribution to the restoration of a spirit of friendship and good will for the people with whom we were not long ago engaged in deadly war, but who we hope, through means like this, may be brought into a wholesome and friendly and lasting relationship with our country and with other democratic and peace-loving countries in a family of nations who desire that their relationship together shall be characterized by friendship, good will and neighbourliness.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with other members in the house and all parts of the house we welcome the opportunity to discuss this treaty. I am sure that throughout the house it is hoped that this treaty may prove beneficial to Canada, beneficial to Japan and beneficial to the world as a means of promoting good will and peace among all men.
As I sat here this afternoon listening to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the exhaustive analysis he gave of both the treaty and matters connected with the formulation of such a treaty, I thought that his speech illustrated the difficulties and, indeed, the contradictions which abound in relationships of this sort in the world at the present time. I think that on a reading of the speech that he has made those contradictions will be quite apparent to the reader, as they were to those who listened to the speech this afternoon.
First, I want to say that I agree with him that it would have been preferable to have referred this treaty to the banking and commerce committee in order that we might investigate it rather more fully. I fancy I heard him say ". . . as we did with the general agreement on tariffs and trade". If he said that then it is not my recollection. My recollection is that the general agreement on tariffs and trade came into this house, the house was called especially to consider it, but it more or less died on the order paper without going to committee. I think it was the intention of the government of the time that it go to committee but I have no recollection of it going there and certainly no recollection of any report coming back or of this house having had an opportunity to approve or disapprove of that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext: The government has never ratified that agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext: No. We have never had an opportunity of expressing approval or disapproval, and the government has never ratified it. I do not think it went to the banking and commerce committee.
