speechtext: It went to the committee but the committee never made a report on it.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
I was just trying to think what happened to it.
As I was saying, there are contradictions in trade relationships, but nevertheless I think the house has to approve of a treaty of this description because, after all, Japan is a great and important nation. My thoughts this afternoon wandered back not only to pre-war years when we were supplying Japan with copper, scrap iron and all the rest of it-material that was used at Pearl Harbor and other places against our own people and own allies-but I was remembering the speeches that were made in this house during the war. I do hope that out of the revived Japan we shall get a democratic Japan; that we shall not get another Japan rearmed and led by militarists once again to become something of a threat to the world, alone or even in co-operation perhaps with others who may threaten the peace of the world at any time. There is no saying what may happen because Japan today is cut off from the markets which she once had as her primary outlets-Manchuria, Korea and China. She is competing for what trade remains in southeast Asia.
As the hon. member for Eglinton said, a population of 85J million people, increasing at the rate of 1-2 million per year-I think that was the figure he gave-occupying a territory two-fifths of the size of British Columbia with only 15 per cent of the whole area arable, is bound to seek both food and outlets for the commodities which it must manufacture in order to obtain both food and raw materials.
For example, in the years 1934-36 manufactures exported from Japan represented 80-7 per cent of the country's exports; 71-6 per cent of the imports by Japan were in the form of foodstuffs and raw materials. That indicates how dependent Japan is for her very existence both on the food with which she must sustain her people and on the exports which she must send abroad in order to pay for the raw materials and the commodities she requires.
We are told that-and this is the year 1952 that I am speaking of-90 per cent of all exports were manufactured goods and that foodstuffs and raw materials accounted for 86 per cent of the imports. All ten of
Trade Agreement with Japan Japan's most important imports are raw materials. Silk is the only raw material exported in quantity. I think that gives a very clear picture of the position in which Japan finds herself. It offers opportunity for Canada-if we can grasp that opportunity. Representing as I do a western and wheat growing area I am, of course, impressed not only with the possibilities of maintaining the market we have established in that country for primary products from the prairie provinces, but also with the possibility of extending those exports.
The demand for Canadian wheat, as the minister indicated this afternoon, has grown steadily over the past several years. The rising demand for wheat products in Japan stems of course first of all from the very rapid increase in population in that country, the changed habits of food that they have acquired in the post-war years and the fact that they have been cut off from the sources of rice upon which they so largely depended in bygone days. The result is, we are told, that not only adults, but more particularly the young people in adolescent years, are becoming accustomed to new cereals, and those new cereals are of particular interest to us because, as the figures produced by the minister and by the hon. member for Eglinton indicated this afternoon, they are wheat and barley, two very important cereal products that we produce in vast quantities in this country.
The United States has been the leading supplier of wheat in the post-war years, but our supplies of wheat to that country have been increased quite markedly. Of course Japan does raise wheat herself, but oviously from the amount of arable land in the country and the fact that rice is grown in large quantities in the country it is certain that Japan will never be able to raise enough food, and particularly cereals, in order to feed herself.
Then of course we are given to understand that over the past few years there has been an increase in meat consumption. To some extent the Japanese have turned from fish to meat for their proteins, and that again means that there is demand for cereals for stock feed and cattle feed, and so we can take that into account.
What our wheat board has to bear in mind is that under the present circumstances, with the amount of cereals available for disposal on the markets of the world, they are in a very competitive area when they try to sell wheat in Japan, and they should do everything possible to promote the sale of it. But it is not only the sale of our wheat that is necessary. If Japan is to buy Canadian
4662	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan raw materials, lumber, minerals, wheat, barley and so on, then she must be enabled to pay for those products, and there is only one way in which nations can pay for the products that they buy, that is by sending abroad something that is saleable and something that will give them the necessary funds with which to pay for their imports. Therefore a trade treaty of this description is of primary importance to the producers of our raw materials in Canada, and, as the hon. member for Eglinton has well emphasized, of primary importance also to the people who work in industries that may be competitive or that may find some competition from the Japanese sources.
When this trade treaty was under discussion, and of course before we knew anything about its contents, in its initial stages I was very pleased to see that the representative of Japan in this city made it very clear on November 3 last that Japan could never balance her trade with Canada even if we gave her lower tariffs. He then went on to say that she would have to reduce the gap between her imports from Canada and her exports. He said:
... if the agreement goes through, Japan likely will be concentrating on Canada's big market for capital goods, rather than on such consumer items as toys, novelties and other sundry items.
And further:
These sundry items, small in price, did not help to boost the total sales figures to Canada by any great amount. Capital goods involve expenditures of great sums of money and thus might help narrow the trade balance gap.
Well, we all hope that that is so. It seems to me that in this treaty the government has attempted that, without raising tariffs, indeed lowering tariffs, because let us bear this in mind that the increase in trade with Japan in the last few years has been an increase under the general tariff, and it is now proposed of course to give Japan the mostfavoured-nation tariffs.
As the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, there are attempts in this treaty to safeguard Canadian industry which might be affected by unfair competition. Unfair competition is very difficult to define. I am one of those who believe that we should do everything we possibly can to remove the barriers to trade across the world, and to give our own people an opportunity of entering world markets as well, at the same time, doing whatever we can to see to it that our producers are not subject to what might be termed unfair competition, though the words "unfair competition" are at best very difficult indeed to define.
It seems to me that this treaty will help to. bring about better relationships and may


give us a better market for certain of our products that of necessity we must send abroad. I noticed the figures given by both the minister and the hon. member for Eglinton of the exports and imports of last year. In round figures our exports to Japan amounted to $119 million worth, and our imports, in round figures again, to about $14 million worth. I also read-I have not it before me, but my recollection is quite clear -the speech that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made in Tokyo when he was visiting there on his world tour. I read that speech very carefully at the time, and I remember the Prime Minister pointed out that while there seems to be a very large gap, $8 for $1 in connection with this trade, yet this does not present a wholly fair picture; that we do import certain Japanese goods indirectly by way of some other countries. Possibly the Prime Minister was thinking of the United States. If that is so, it would help our trade relationships with Japan if we could import those commodities directly into this country, Japan thereby earning Canadian dollars instead of United States' dollars with which the Japanese importers could purchase Canadian goods. I hope that that may be one result of this treaty.
There are a number of provisions in the treaty, which I am not going into because the hon. member for Eglinton went into them very thoroughly, which may be applied, duties which may be applied and evaluations which may be applied, and so forth. The main interest that any of us can have in this treaty is that we hope it will promote the welfare of Canada as well as of course the welfare of the people of Japan; that it will be mutually beneficial; and in spite of the fears that have been expressed this afternoon, we are doing the proper thing in approving of this treaty today and giving it at least a fair trial.
I know it can be said, and said quite accurately and truthfully, that prior to the second world war certain unfair trade practices were indulged in by Japan. A couple of weeks ago, while doing a little packing for storage purposes, I had a look at some china and I noticed on one piece the quite large letters "U.S." and then very small letters "Pat"-"United States patent", and almost so small that you had to have pretty powerful glasses to read the little word underneath "Japan". You would imagine if you picked it up casually and took a look at it that it was of U.S. manufacture. Those people from British Columbia will recollect how there were certain cans of fish marked "Can" and most people thought that that was indicative of an article produced in

Canada and of course it was not. Now the Japanese government agrees to discontinue these unfair trade practices. I hope that if we indulged in any unfair trade practices ourselves that we too will undertake to do away with them.
A short time ago I brought to the attention of the house weaknesses in our legislation regarding the marking of countries of origin, and the new act has now been proclaimed. I hope it will have some effect at least in this particular matter.
However, in spite of the fears which have been expressed, fears which I know are legitimately held by the workers, for example, in the textile industry, I hope these fears will be unfounded and that we may find this treaty of benefit to all classes of producers in Canada, because there is one thing to be said and that is that if we have prosperous producers in one field of industry, then that in the main is reflected in other fields of industry. If our western farmers are able to dispose of their cereals advantageously then they have money with which to buy, not Japanese textiles, but large quantities of Canadian textiles, although they may still buy a small number of textiles originating in Japan. In other words, I hope a treaty of this description will assist the health of the entire economy of this country. I do not wish to repeat what the hon. member for Eglinton has said. I know he will not misunderstand me when I say he has put before us all the contradictions to be found in trading relations of this description. But I hope we may straighten out these contradictions and find this treaty mutually beneficial to Canada and to Japan.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with real interest this afternoon to the speeches made by the minister and the spokesmen of the other two parties in connection with the agreement on commerce between Canada and Japan. As I listened to those speeches I could not escape the feeling that it is terribly difficult, when we come to consider matters of trade and commerce, to lay down any hard and fast rule which will work successfully in all cases for our people. I hope I shall not be guilty, therefore, of trying to lay down any hard and fast rule in connection with what I shall have to say this afternoon.
I was very pleased to see that Canada has not treated Japan as vanquished countries have so often been treated after wars in the past. I take real satisfaction out of the fact that Canada, through this treaty and in other ways, is according to the Japanese people the kind of honourable treatment which ought to be extended to them by a
Trade Agreement with Japan mature people with a well developed social conscience, and I do believe that that is the kind of treatment Canadians are according to the Japanese people.
I have examined the terms of the agreement most carefully. I have listened to the speeches made this afternoon by the minister and the hon. members who followed him. It seems to me that the agreement adequately safeguards Canada's interests. I say that because I discovered through my reading of the treaty that British preferences are not interfered with, and we are free to apply dumping duties in the event that Japan at any time should resort to dumping goods on to our market at unreasonable prices. It just occurs to me though how absurd the world situation is when we have to cry out against being able to buy things too cheaply. However, there it is; it is just one of those absurdities you come across when you talk about the world of trade.
Coming back to the safeguards which I think are in the treaty, though the mostfavoured-nation principle occupies a prominent part of the agreement escape clauses have been provided which make it possible for either party to apply trade or exchange restrictions if necessary in order to safeguard its external financial position and balance of payments.
I would like to comment just briefly on the most-favoured-nation principle. That principle plays a very prominent part in the treaty. It is included in article I, as a matter of fact. Now, this is sometimes called nondiscrimination, and in my experience a good many people have been bowled over by the sound and connotation of that expression "non-discrimination" and they chew on it, adhere to it, or so they say, with almost religious zeal and fanaticism. But what they do not seem to realize is that the unconditional, and I emphasize that, most-favourednation principle was invented by the United States as a means of completely destroying the British preferential system so that whenever it suited her purpose she could break into the game and with her great industrial power dominate world trade.
The United States has demanded the acceptance and the inclusion of the unconditional most-favoured-nation principle in all international trade treaties and agreements for many years. All during that time, strangely enough, she has been striving with all her might, and one can say with her magnificent capacity, to make herself self-sufficient. Now, if you ever want some contradictions take a look at that. Today, the United States, for all practical purposes, is in that position of self-sufficiency. All during the days when

Trade Agreement with Japan Great Britain, Germany and Japan exported goods to the amount of no less than 20 per cent of their total national income, the United States was exporting only six per cent gross, and if inter-company relationships were eliminated from that six per cent the total of her exports would not be more than about three per cent of her national income.
I cite these figures only to show that while most countries in the world have continually to depend upon foreign trade to a very large degree and therefore have done nothing to adjust their thinking toward the development of home markets, the United States was moving deliberately and rapidly toward a position of self-sufficiency, in which position she would not have to depend to a very large extent on foreign trade.
The other nations were blind to what was going on, or they appeared to be; and therefore the unconditional most-favoured-nation principle was slipped over on them. But since the adoption of the unconditional mostfavoured-nation clause in trade treaties, we have operated on the escape clauses more than on the principle itself. It appears that in the present agreement with Japan provision has been made to continue on this line, namely operation on the escape clauses more than on the principle.
The agreement we are considering is, in reality, a bilateral agreement including the qualified most-favoured-nation clause. I was particularly glad to find that we did not insist upon inserting in this treaty the unconditional most-favoured-nation treatment. That fact indicates that we are really ready and willing to give the Japanese people a reasonable chance in the world of trade.
Finally, the present treaty expresses Canada's right to apply export or import restrictions under our security legislation. It therefore seems to me that there is little to worry about so far as the wording of the treaty is concerned. How it will work out in the future we do not know at the present time. We certainly hope that it will work out well. I notice, however, that one of the terms of the treaty is that it shall stand for one year and after that period can be terminable upon three months' notice by either party. Hence it is not a thing which could not be corrected if we found conditions under it growing intolerable.
Many Canadian people are showing some concern lest the agreement with Japan result in harm to them and to industrial enterprises in this country. What are we to say to these people? For example, a few days ago I received from certain toy manufacturers in Canada a letter in which they complained

about the possibility of harm to their industries under this treaty. The question is this: What are we going to say to such groups as that?
In the first place, the agreement itself says that either party may deviate temporarily from the terms of paragraphs 1 and 2 to prevent undue damage to the industries of either country through the full application of the terms of the treaty. That provision in itself is some safeguard. In the second place, I think we ought to keep in our minds the thought that to be fair in this world today we must adopt a policy of "live and let live". Certainly that should be the cardinal principle of all our external relations. Japan therefore must be allowed her proper place in the world of trade and must be allowed an amount of trade which will make it possible for her people to find employment and to live on a decent standard.
The terms of the trade agreement are not, in my opinion, more generous towards Japan than they should be. We ought to have regard to what was done to Japan by the peace treaty which was signed in 1951, if I am not mistaken. Let us not forget also that Japan felt she had been forced to resort to war in order to break out of unbearable restrictions that, over the years, had been imposed upon her trade before 1340 or 1941. I have read statements by high-placed Japanese in the pre-war years which definitely point to a feeling of aggravation at those restrictions, particularly the restrictions placed upon Japan by the unconditional mostfavoured-nation clause.
I am conscious of the fact that for many years perhaps Japan practised unfair trade arrangements; that is, she resorted to unfair trade practices. That matter has already been stressed by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) this afternoon. But they had the feeling-and they have expressed it in no uncertain terms-that they had to resort to force in order to break out of the extremely vicious type of aggravating restrictions placed upon them in their trade relations prior to 1941.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we should also be reminded that the treaty of peace signed with Japan in 1951 substantially reduced Japanese territory. As I pointed out at the time when we were discussing that peace treaty, that reduction was exceedingly serious as it had left 85 million people with not nearly enough land on which to produce the food they needed. Some of the richest and most important rice-producing areas were taken from them, a circumstance which doubtless accounts for the fact that in this

past year they have been importing substantial amounts of wheat and barley from Canada.
I was well pleased to hear the minister say this afternoon that Japan had become our third largest customer so far as wheat is concerned and that she had also bought substantial amounts of barley from us. In these and other things Japan is now and, in my judgment, can continue to be for many years, one of our best customers. She is nearest to our great Pacific ports from which we export great quantities of cereal grains. However, we in this group adhere to the principle that trade must be a two-way street. The Canadian people should take note of the fact that last year we bought from Japan, according to the minister's own words this afternoon, only 30 cents' worth out of each $100 worth of our Canadian imports. That is a fairly small figure for imports from a country that is our third best wheat customer.
I agree with the minister that there is plenty of room for imports into Canada from Japan. Indeed if we want to cultivate markets in Japan for our products, we must buy Japanese goods in return. As was said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that is the only way in which the Japanese people can pay for the things they want to buy from us. It is of particular importance that we cultivate a permanent market for our wheat. I say "particular" in the light of the huge carryover from previous years that we have in Canada of cereal grains. Japan is and always has been seriously short of food materials, particularly good cereal grains and proteins. When I mention proteins, let me say that perhaps the years ahead may see an expansion of our exports to Japan of protein foods if we make wise use of the opportunities afforded by the agreement we are now considering and of the concessions granted to Canada under that treaty.
Those concessions spoken of by the minister this afternoon put the Canadian producer into a fair competitive position in Japan. Those Canadians who oppose the ratification of the treaty-and I suppose there will be a number of them-should be told that, generally speaking, a fair-competition policy will handle the situation for them as it will for everybody else. We put forward the view that our aim should be to build up in Canada a balanced economy, one wherein agriculture and industry are in fair balance. We think that is the safest type of economy in all times-in wartime and in peacetime- and the most useful type in a world which so often is the scene of conflict and strife.
Trade Agreement with Japan It therefore seems that we must have in Canada more industry employing more people. But of course the big question everybody asks is this: What industry?
Again we face a problem of trying to lay down something like a hard and fast rule, but we cannot do it. Therefore we have to be guided by considerations of the time and of the circumstances under which we live. There are, it seems to me, those industries which are absolutely essential at all times, in wartime and in peacetime. There are those industries that are essential in times of war and of world dislocation, but perhaps only desirable in times of peace. Then there are those that are essential neither in time of peace or war. These could be called desirable just the same as the others if they turn out useful goods and services and give employment to our people under fair conditions.
But in any case where any of these industries do put pressure on the government for protection against Japanese fair competition in our market, we think that the government should most carefully examine the whole situation in each individual case to make sure that we do not in any case militate against Canadian consumers by extending protection to industries that have not done their utmost to keep down their costs to efficient levels by every means possible, including the plowing back of a substantial part of their profits into plant improvement and modernization. Here again, Mr. Speaker, I say that it is pretty difficult to lay down any hard and fast rule, but that at least seems to be the expression of a principle that might guide us in determining what should be done in any case where an industry feels that it is in danger as a consequence of this treaty.
We are likely to hear protests from the textile industries. How are we going to treat those protests? That is another question, and certainly it is hard for me to say what should be done. But I remind the house that some years ago the government of Canada established what was known as the Stevens committee to investigate the textile industries and others. It had to do with price spreads and that sort of thing. The Stevens committee discovered that Canadian textile industries were inefficient. They paid poor wages and took large profits, little of which was turned back to modernize plants and keep them up to date.
It seems to me that kind of industry does not deserve protection against fair competition at the expense of the Canadian consumer. Maybe the situation has changed. It may possibly be that the Canadian textile industries have improved the whole situation since

Trade Agreement with Japan the days of the Stevens investigation, and if so consideration should be given to that fact. But let me emphasize again that the government should not be pressured into extending protection to any industry without the fullest consideration of all the facts and careful measurement of the value to our country and the world of those industries, as well as the position in which our consumers would be put as a consequence of what might be done.
We are not forgetting, Mr. Speaker, that the success of this treaty, as well as the health and vigour of Canadian industry, will depend very largely on how we put our own house in order. There must be a careful and critical review of our taxation structure to ascertain what effect our taxes are having on costs and on our competitive position. I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that as we enter this period of intensive competition with countries like Japan, Germany and others that have revived wonderfully from the effects of war we have got to be more cost conscious than ever before in our lives. Consequently it seems to me every effort should be made to reduce taxes, especially those that are imposed on commodities and that pyramid costs and push up prices.
To be in a healthy condition our home markets should constantly be in possession of adequate purchasing power to enable the Canadian people to purchase all of the production of Canada if they want to buy it. In that favourable position we can, when we export goods to Japan or any other country, import goods of equal over-all value from those countries with confidence that these imports can be sold and used by our people. Under circumstances like that we would not have to resort to the practice of maintaining unfavourable trade balances at the expense of other countries, and therefore one of the main causes of war would be removed.
I think it might have been wise to have the agreement considered by the banking and commerce committee, and perhaps the minister may yet agree to have that done. In any event we think that the treaty does adequately safeguard Canada's interests while at the same time giving Japan a chance for a fair share of our trade. Consequently we approve ratification, and in approving it we express the hope that the treaty will be one of the big factors in cultivating peace, good will, security and prosperity in the Pacific area and in the whole world.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. W. A. White (Waterloo South):
subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on the Japanese trade agreement because I feel that the agreement when it is ratified will


have a far-reaching effect on many industries in this country, chief among which is the textile industry. In my maiden speech last year I attempted to direct the attention of the house to the decrease in the number of people employed in the fourteen textile mills in Galt, Preston and Hespeler, and since that time the situation has not improved but has grown gradually worse. In the year 1950 the textile industry in Canada which is composed of two branches, primary textiles and secondary textiles, employed approximately 200,000 people or one-sixth of our total industrial labour force. This industry is therefore one of the largest employers of industrial labour in Canada.
The number of people employed in the primary textile industry has gradually dwindled until today there are less than 82,000 textile workers employed in this branch of the industry in Canada, and a large number of these are on short time. During the past number of months nineteen textile mills have closed their doors and it is very doubtful if any of them will ever open again under present conditions. A number of the larger mills are located in large industrial cities and undoubtedly many of the unemployed textile workers in these centres have since been absorbed in other industries, but the majority of the textile plants are located in small communities and are the main source of employment. Such is the case in the town of Hespeler in my riding. In this small town, with a population of 3,400 people, there were 1,415 people employed in 1950 in the Dominion Woollens and Worsteds mill and the Artex mill whereas today there are only 847 people working in these two plants, and they are on short time.
While I was home during the Christmas recess workers and management voluntarily accepted a 13 per cent cut in wages to help keep the Dominion Woollens and Worsteds mill operating. Many of the employees of this mill have their whole life savings tied up in their homes in the town of Hespeler, and the closing of this mill would cause them to lose everything that they have worked for. This was a sincere effort on the part of management and employees to protect their jobs and their homes by this action. In addition, the entire business life of this community is almost entirely dependent on these mills continuing to operate. I know from communications that I have received from the board of trade of Hespeler, as well as the workers, that they are not too optimistic about the future of the textile industry under conditions as they exist today.

What has happened to the textile industry in Canada? Certainly any suggestion that the industry has overexpanded or is inefficient in my opinion is not borne out by the facts. In the period from 1935 to 1939 the textile industry in Canada was supplying 73 per cent of the domestic market. In 1950, with full employment, this industry was only able to supply 68 per cent of the domestic market. I do not believe, therefore, that the suggestion the industry has overexpanded is true. These statistics establish, in my opinion, that with the increase in population and the increase in purchasing power of the Canadian people the textile industry was not able to supply as large a portion of the domestic market in 1950, even with full employment, as it was able to supply in the years from 1935 to 1939.
It was pointed out also in this house by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) that the textile industry had spent $450 million for modern equipment since the end of world war II, bringing the production of the industry to the highest point of efficiency. Any suggestion that the textile industry in inefficient, therefore, is in my opinion not a valid one. The amount of textiles being purchased in Canada has been increasing each year since 1950, yet the amount of textiles supplied by the Canadian mills has gradually dwindled until today the textile mills in Canada are only sharing the domestic market to the extent of 51 per cent. I can only conclude from this information that the depressed condition in which the textile industry finds itself today is, to a large extent, due to the ever-increasing quantities of imported textiles being sold on the Canadian market.
The Canadian textile industry faces competition from cottons and synthetic materials from the United States and Japan, while their competition in woollens and worsteds comes from the United Kingdom and the rest of Europe. The average rate of wages paid textile workers in the United States is $1.37 per hour, compared with $1.11 per hour in Canada. This difference in wages, with the addition of the present rate of duty applied against the American textiles, is offset to a large extent by the fact that the United States manufacturers have a potential market ten times greater than the Canadian industry, which is limited almost entirely to the domestic market because of the higher rates of duties prevailing in other countries.
The United States textile manufacturer, with his greater potential market, will run off an average of 100,000 yards of one material, whereas the Canadian textile mill will have only an average run of 1,000 yards.
83276-296J
Trade Agreement with. Japan This, in itself, increases the production costs of the Canadian industry by approximately 35 per cent, because after each run of cloth it is necessary to make certain changes and to clean all the cards. The Canadian textile manufacturer is also confronted with another type of competition from the United States. It is the dumping of surplus goods. I was very glad this government recognized that this unfair trade practice existed, and took steps to correct the situation by the passing of Bill No. 29 at this session.
As I stated before, the Canadian textile industry is also confronted with competition in the field of cottons and synthetics from Japan, where the average hourly rate of wage is 13-9 cents per hour as compared with $1.11 cents per hour in Canada. This competition is serious enough with the present rate of duty, and will become more serious if Japan is given most-favoured-nation treatment. The Canadian textile mills are now facing competition in the fields of woollens and worsteds from the United Kingdom, where the hourly rate of wages is approximately 40 cents per hour and from other countries in Europe where even less wages' are paid.
I know that there are many reasons why a trade agreement with Japan is necessary.
I know that last year Japan bought Canadian wheat and other primary products, as-well as some of our natural resources, to the. value of $119 million, and that Canada purchased during the same period from Japan only $14 million worth of the goods that Japan had to sell. It is quite obvious that Japan cannot continue indefinitely with such an unfavourable balance of trade with this country. I recognize also that Japan is the one bulwark of democracy in that part of the world. If we refuse to trade with her on some fair basis, we would inevitably be driving her into the hands of the communists.
I am convinced, however, that if Canada and Canadians are going to continue to enjoy, the second highest standard of living in the world, then there will have to be a complete revision of our tariffs in relation to-those countries where wages are so much lower than our own. If that is not done we will be confronted with more and more industrial unemployment. In my opinion it would be a backward step to lower our standard of living in order to compete with these nations. The member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), in his speech during the budget debate on April 13, 1954, as recorded at page 4036 of Hansard, said:
If you want to correct unemployment in Canada, put some purchasing power in the pockets of
4668	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan
western farmers. Take steps to buy their grain, and in my opinion there will be no unemployment in a matter of a few short months.
The western farmer is no different from anyone else, and if he can buy imported goods cheaper than he can buy Canadian-made goods he is going to do so. This scheme is not going to correct industrial unemployment in this country. No Canadian industry can ever hope to compete with manufactured goods in those countries in which the wages paid are so much lower than those paid in the Canadian industry, no matter how much the industry improves its efficiency or methods of production. The impact of competition in manufactured goods from these low-wage countries is being felt by some other industries in Canada in addition to the textile industry.
Another such industry is the machine tool industry in this country, which was so important to Canada's war effort. The Canada Machinery Corporation in the city of Galt, which normally employs 300 or more persons, now has a payroll of only 90 people, and the R. McDougall Company is equally hard hit. There is no doubt in my mind that Japan has a substantial machine tool industry because such an industry was very essential in order for her to participate in the last world war. Since the machine tool industry in Canada is in a depressed condition from competition with the low wage countries in Europe where skilled mechanics get 50 cents or less per hour compared to $1.62 an hour paid in Canada, it would seem to me that any large imports of machine tools to this country from Japan would almost be a final blow from which the industry would find it exceedingly difficult to recover.
The devaluation of the pound and the premium commanded by the Canadian dollar has had the effect of reducing the present tariffs still further. Therefore I would suggest that the tariff board should be authorized and instructed to review our entire tariff structure in the light of conditions as they exist today in order to determine what impact foreign manufactured goods, especially those from low wage countries, have on our domestic industries. I believe that this should be done as soon as possible so that the government will have this information before it when the general agreement on tariffs and trade comes up for review next year.
In going over the Japanese trade agreement I was very glad to see that the agreement is only for one year and can be terminated by either of the contracting parties on three months' notice at the end of the year. I was also very pleased to see that in this agreement there was included an escape clause


which allows Canada to place its own values for duty purposes on any Japanese products which, as a result of the said agreement, are being imported into Canada in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to threaten serious injury to Canadian producers of competitive products.
This agreement secures for Canada another potential market for its primary products and natural resources which is very desirable, but in return Canada has extended mostfavoured-nation tariffs to Japanese manufactured goods which in effect applies the same rates of duty against Japanese manufactured goods as are at present applied against manufactured goods from the United States and other nations who are included in the general agreement on tariffs and trade. This places Japan in a preferred position in competition for the Canadian market since the wages paid in their country are so much lower than those paid in the United States and other countries of Europe. Even if the escape clause is used it only means that Canadian industry has another competitor for its domestic market in the same category as the low wage countries of Europe.
I therefore repeat again and strongly urge that the tariff board should be directed and instructed to investigate our entire system of tariffs in order to determine the impact imports from low wage countries have on our domestic industries so that with this information adjustments can be made in our tariffs that will permit Canadian industries to have an opportunity at least to compete in our domestic market with manufactured goods imported into Canada from countries where wages are so much lower than in our own.
In my opinion we would then be creating an economic climate in our country which would permit industry and agriculture to prosper side by side.

subtopic: CANADA-JAPAN  RATIFICATION OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA MARCH 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity at this stage of the debate to say a few words of a general nature in support of the government's action in entering into the trade agreement with Japan. My reasons for so doing stem from several considerations, foremost among which are our export trade and our continued resistance to the expansion of communism in eastern Europe and Asia.
Japan in the last war was one of our bitterest enemies and fought us and our allies with all the resources at her disposal. Upon the termination of the war, on September 8, 1951, the treaty of peace was signed with Japan at the city of San Francisco. This treaty was the subject of considerable criticism throughout the western world but

the wisdom shown in pressing for its finalization has justified this action on the part of the western allies.
As a result of this treaty the western world has gone along with Japan and assisted her in rehabilitating herself in a democratic manner.
We must not forget that following the war and it is no secret that even today the peoples of Japan are divided as to where their loyalties should extend and to what extent they should participate in world affairs. The first minority group in Japan consists of the communists who urge the newly elected Japanese parliament to break its ties with the west, refute the San Francisco peace treaty, reject its present mutual defence assistance agreement with the United States and line up with the communist-dominated peoples of Asia.
The second group-the neutralists or right wing of the socialist party-advocates an isolationist policy whereby Japan would take no part in world affairs. This obviously is not a practical solution to their problem in view of their geographical position and the present state of world affairs.
The other group, which is by far the largest, favours a rejection of the communists' attempt to make Japan another satellite of Russia and China. Japan, situate as it is close to the shores of Asia, cannot be neutral but if it is to stand against communist aggression and expansion in the East it will require the military and economic support of the United States, Canada and the other western powers.
Hon. members know from their personal experience that many lasting, trustful and valuable personal friendships are created among individuals as a result of business and professional association. In their daily contacts they get to know those whom they can trust and to what extent. I think a parallel can be drawn in international relations. The hand of friendship has been extended to Japan by the western world. It has been gratefully accepted. This was particularly evidenced when our Prime Minister visited that country on his world tour, where not only was he met by the Japanese dignitaries but also by the school children who lined the streets in an expression of friendly welcome.
It is my opinion that friendly trade relations with Japan will do more than anything else to convince the Japanese people that we are sincere in our desire to have Japan as an ally; that we are prepared to assist her in her resistance to communist domination and welcome her membership in the fraternity of free and democratic nations. In
Trade Agreement with Japan the last war we found that Japan was a power to be reckoned with and no opportunity should be lost to encourage her alignment with the West in the world power struggle.
The considerations so far enumerated would be enough in my opinion to justify the entry of Canada into a trade agreement with Japan, but there is another very important consideration and that is our need for foreign markets. In Canada, which is so dependent on international trade, every sensible person wants more trade with everybody. There is no doubt that more than any other country in the world we depend on our foreign trade for our prosperity. The United States, which is the only other country of the world with a standard of living comparable to ours, relies for her prosperity on exports to the extent of only about four per cent, whereas Canada is dependent upon her exports for about 30 per cent of her national income.
To agriculture our continuity of trade is of paramount importance. Our wheat crop is now averaging in excess of 500 million bushels of which domestic consumption, including grain used for seed and feed, would not exceed 140 million bushels. Of a crop of 136 million bushels of oats we exported 65 million bushels, and of a crop of 176 million bushels of barley we exported 119 million bushels. In addition to the export of grain, substantial stocks of other farm and dairy products have been exported to other countries to add to our national income.
In addition to the export of farm products, our exports of minerals, processed and manufactured goods have been substantial. The export of these commodities is very important, not only to agriculture but also to labour and to industry.
Since the war our trade with Japan has grown steadily and at the risk of repetition I would say that in the calendar year 1953 our exports to Japan totalled $118,500,000 while our imports amounted to $13,600,000. Our chief sales to Japan consisted of $52,433,562 of wheat, $17,496,915 of barley, $7,014,280 of pulp, $1,380,565 of grass seed and other lesser items. In the year 1953-54 Japan's crop quota was 36,744,000 bushels. She had purchased from Canada to April 30 of this year 11,690,000 bushels of wheat. This, together with purchases from the United States, has almost filled her quota. This figure includes only purchases registered under the international wheat agreement and information available indicates that other sales outside the agreement have been made. Since April 30, 14 further cargoes have been sold, which at 350,000 bushels per cargo, would amount to approximately 5 million further bushels, bringing the total well over
4670	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with Japan 17 million bushels to date with the remainder of the year's purchases to be anticipated. These facts, together with the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to the effect that "steps have been taken to safeguard the position of Canada in the Japanese market for the next two years" furnish, I believe, sufficient evidence to justify a favourable and optimistic attitude in regard to our future trade with Japan.
On this occasion I would like to take the opportunity to commend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) upon his work, the work of his department and the *agencies under his direction, for their increasing vigilance and their aggressive policy in seeking markets for our products. The department's trade representatives in foreign countries have been doing a tremendous job of promoting Canadian sales. In addition the wheat board has maintained a vigorous policy of seeking out and maintaining markets for our grains.
A Canadian grain and flour mission of the Canadian 'wheat board, headed by Mr. Riddel, recently returned from a tour of the Asiatic countries where they had been seeking markets for our Canadian grain. The delegation was well received in Japan and found that Canadian wheat was very well liked, particularly in relation to quality which they found to be better than the average quality of American wheat they had been receiving, and all indications were that Japan would continue to be a good market for Canadian wheat in the years to come.
Factors which have contributed toward the popularity of wheat products in Japan in preference to rice have been, firstly, the shortage of fuel for cooking purposes in the homes and, secondly, the fact that many Japanese women are occupied in working during the day. Bread is a much more convenient form of food by reason of these considerations and is growing in popularity. It, therefore, seems reasonable to assume that our wheat market in Japan is established and that in the course of time it will increase, provided Japan can obtain the foreign currency to purchase our products. A similar consideration applies to barley. Our exports in the past year of barley were valued at $17 million and the prospects of increasing our exports to Japan of this commodity are also >very good.
Our great exporting industries are also searching for larger outlets and industries in British Columbia have again taken the initiative as they did in the matter of marketing their fish products, and a delegation of the Vancouver board of trade, including an
[Mr. Weselak.l

official representative of the British Columbia government, went to Tokyo early in April to seek new markets for Canadian goods. The prospect of obtaining further markets are bright. A recent estimate in Foreign Trade, a government publication, showed that Japan is urgently in need of over three million housing units to ease the serious housing shortage in Japan. Assuming that the average two or three-room house requires about 7,000 board feet of lumber, then, a market exists for a considerable amount of Canadian lumber. There is no doubt that if the needs of the Japanese people were given careful study other buyers could be found for many Canadian products and raw materials.
We must face the fact that if Japan is to continue buying from Canada at her present rate, or if as may well be, her imports from this country are to increase, then she must sell more to Canada. I believe this agreement is a recognition of this fact and a step toward retaining this market which we have had the good fortune to obtain. If the agreement has the effect of more Japanese goods being imported into Canada, which will likely be the result, they necessarily must compete with the Canadian manufacturers and indications are that this competition will be felt mainly in the toy, textile and electrical products which Japan can make much cheaper than can our Canadian manufacturers.
One of the terms of the agreement, incorporated by way of a communication addressed to the ambassador of Japan from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), dated March 31, 1954, and set QUt in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons for Wednesday, March 31, 1954, at page 7 of the addendum, provides, and I quote:
1.	Ii, as a result of unforeseen developments and of the effect of the obligations incurred by Canada under the aforesaid agreement, any product is being imported into its territory in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic producers in its territory of like or directly competitive products, Canada will be free, in respect of such product, and to the extent and for such a time as may be necessary to prevent or remedy such injury, to establish values for ordinary and special duty purposes.
2.	In determining whether values should be established in respect of any product pursuant to paragraph 1 and in determining the level at which such values should be established, Canada will take into account the prices of like or directly competitive products, if any, being imported at that time from other countries.
The inclusion of the right of Canada to establish values for ordinary and special duty purposes for the purpose of preventing

serious injury to domestic producers of competitive products, together with the provisions relating to unfair trade practices, provides industries affected with an adequate safeguard against indiscriminate competition from Japanese imports. This power will have to be exercised by the government with great care in accordance with the spirit of the agreement and in such a manner as to promote the national interest.
Large surpluses of goods, especially agricultural products, hang over the market. We must maintain our present huge trade in other markets, and that is our basic problem. This problem will not be cured but will be greatly worsened by restricting the international trade on which this nation largely lives, and therefore I urge the government on this occasion to exercise the power reserved to it in the agreement only when conditions warrant their use and, if possible, sparingly, but always in the interest of the Canadian economy as a whole.
In conclusion I would like to emphasize that this trade pact is not only a trade agreement as such; it is a symbol of Japan's desire to join the fraternity of nations in the free world, to work with them in friendly co-operation toward a solution of the grave problems which face the world today. Our government, in negotiating this trade treaty, has accepted the fact that Japan must sooner or later live by her own exports; that she cannot subsist upon voluntary gifts, nor can she carry on the one-sided exchange of goods which has been the case in the past. The Japanese people must be assured that their alliance with the West is not only sound in military strategy but assures them a tolerable life.

Motion agreed to.
